titre: The Jamaican mongoose solved the rat problem, then created a tick invasion
accroche: A planter imports nine mongooses in 1872 to save his sugarcane fields. He was right about the rats, and wrong about almost everything else.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1871, William Bancroft Espeut loses part of his sugarcane crop to rats, on his Spring Garden estate in Jamaica. His wife, who had lived in Ceylon, remembers having seen an Indian mongoose kill rats there and suggests it to him. Espeut writes to the colonial government, obtains permission after several refusals, and on February 13, 1872, receives, by the ship Merchantman, nine mongooses from Calcutta: four males and five females, for nine pounds sterling. He releases them in his fields, in four batches.

## A claimed success

In less than six months, by his own account read in 1882 before the Zoological Society of London, the rats are markedly less destructive. In two years, the cost of fighting rats has almost vanished. Espeut himself puts the benefit to the island at more than one hundred fifty thousand pounds a year, and cites the government botanist Morris, who for his part estimates it at no less than one hundred thousand pounds a year; he also cites cocoa exports, which rose from 311 hundredweight in 1875 to 3,304 hundredweight in 1880, as proof that crops previously ravaged become possible again. Within a few years, the mongoose spreads across the whole island, trapped and resold by the inhabitants to neighboring planters, who in turn introduce it to Grenada, Barbados, and elsewhere in the West Indies.

Espeut notes nonetheless, in that same text, that quail and other ground-nesting birds have declined.

## What the mongoose actually did

The mongoose eats unselectively: its diet also includes birds, small mammals, and seeds, but invertebrates and lizards alone make up, according to more recent studies, about 93% of it, with rats only a fraction. Within a few decades, several Jamaican species disappear or become impossible to find: the Blue Mountain duck is declared extinct, the limpkin survives in only a single spot on the island around 1910. A committee convened by the governor in 1890 concludes that the mongoose caused the extinction of several birds and recommends banning any further introduction of species. Deprived of some of their natural predators, ticks proliferate to the point of harassing livestock; in 1896, a visiting British administrator finds, set beside his bed, a bowl of oil and a feather, intended for removing them from the skin.

## What shifts

The mongoose did not even keep its initial promise to the end. As early as 1888, a coffee planter settled in Jamaica after having practiced in Ceylon observes that the animal, grown hard to catch, no longer kills as many rats as before. The problem the mongoose was meant to solve did not disappear; it merely changed scale, and the solution imported for a single pest produced another that no one had foreseen.

carte.punch: Nine mongooses imported in 1872 solved a rat problem, and brought on a tick invasion.
carte.idee: A Jamaican planter introduces nine Indian mongooses in 1872 to protect his sugarcane. The rats recede, but the mongoose also decimates the island's birds and reptiles, to the point of extinction for several species. Deprived of their predators, ticks in turn proliferate.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Holmes (2023), “A plague of weasels and ticks,” full text
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The complete story, from the motives for the introduction to the colonial naturalists' rationalization of the disaster.

quiz.question: Why did the introduction of the mongoose end up causing a proliferation of ticks in Jamaica?
choix: Because the mongoose also eats the ticks' natural predators and their usual hosts
Because the mongoose itself carries ticks in its fur
Because the mongoose was imported along with ticks, by mistake
Because the disappearance of the rats left more food available for the ticks
quiz.explication: The mongoose decimated the insect-eating birds and reptiles that naturally regulated the ticks. It does not itself carry these parasites and was not imported with them; it is the disappearance of its own prey, predators of the ticks, that allowed them to proliferate.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who suggested to Espeut that he import the mongoose to his estate?
choix: The government botanist, tasked with estimating the economic benefit
The colonial governor, after a scientific report on pests
His wife, who had seen a mongoose kill rats in Ceylon
A neighboring planter, who had already imported some for his own fields
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It was Espeut's wife, who had lived in Ceylon and had seen an Indian mongoose kill rats there, who suggested this solution to him; Morris, the botanist, comes in only afterward to estimate the benefit.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the more recent studies cited by Holmes (2023), what does the mongoose mainly eat in Jamaica?
choix: Rats, for the bulk of its diet
Invertebrates and lizards, for about 93% of its diet
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the studies cited by Holmes, invertebrates and lizards alone make up about 93% of the mongoose's diet; rats are only a fraction of it, despite the animal's reputation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the committee convened by the governor of Jamaica in 1890 recommend?
choix: Importing more mongooses to fight the ticks
Continuing the studies without changing anything
Banning any further introduction of species
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After finding that the mongoose had caused the extinction of several birds, the committee convened by the governor in 1890 recommended banning any further introduction of animal species.
